name: Aji Amarillo

name: Ajowan

Dry roasting Ajowan or frying it in oil mellows the flavour and brings out a caraway taste.

name: Aleppo Chiles

name: Allspice

It does, however get its name from the fact that it tastes somewhat like a peppery blend of cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. Allspice loses its flavour very quickly when ground, its recommend to buy whole berries and grinding them yourself just before using.

name: Ancho Chiles
notes: When a ripe poblano pepper is dried, it becomes an ancho chile. Anchos are quite mild and are used in all kinds of traditional Mexican cooking. Anchos are deep red-brown and have a wonderful, sweet raisiny flavour that provide lots of personality to food without a lot of heat. These are the most commonly used chile in Mexico.

name: Birch Bark
notes: Birch Bark, a spice and herb used in beer brewing, adds a unique flavor profile to the final product. With its distinct earthy and slightly sweet taste, Birch Bark influences the taste of beer by imparting subtle notes of wintergreen, mint, and even leather. This natural ingredient is often used for its aromatic qualities and ability to enhance complexity in various beer styles. Apart from adding flavor, Birch Bark has several properties that make it beneficial for brewing. It contains compounds such as betulinic acid and methyl salicylate which contribute to its characteristic aroma and potential health benefits. Additionally, the antimicrobial properties found in Birch Bark can aid in preserving the freshness of beers during fermentation. Typically utilized in craft breweries or homebrewing settings, Birch Bark finds application in different beer styles including stouts/porters, saisons/farmhouse ales, and gruits (herb-infused beers). Its addition can add depth to dark beers like stouts by complementing their roasty flavors with hints of herbal sweetness. In saisons or farmhouse ales where wild yeast strains are frequently employed for fermentation, Birch Bark contributes an intriguing layer of complexity alongside other spices like coriander or black pepper. Gruits benefit from this botanical ingredient as well because it imparts an earthy quality that aligns with their historical use of herbs instead of hops as bittering agents.

name: Mace
notes: Mace is possibly the most interesting and unique of all spices. It?s a little-known fact that mace is from the same seed pod that gives us nutmeg. While nutmeg is the inner seed of the pod, mace is the lacy reddish net that surrounds the outside of the shell. During harvest, the mace is removed whole and dried, at which point it is known as a blade. Mace is very similar to nutmeg in flavour and scent, though a little more delicate and sweet. It is also more expensive, since there is so much less of it in each pod.

White peppercorns contain less essential oil than black peppercorns, as this is in the skin, so they have less aroma and a sweetish pungency to them.

name: Rooibos
notes: Typical color range: 52-70 EBC (typical 61) Rooibos, a popular South African herbal tea, has found its way into the world of beer brewing and is making quite an impact. Known for its distinct flavor profile that includes sweet, nutty notes with hints of caramel and vanilla, Rooibos adds complexity and depth to beer. Its unique taste is influencing the overall flavor by providing a malty sweetness that balances out bitterness or hoppy flavors in beers. The properties of Rooibos make it suitable for various applications in brewing. It can be used as an ingredient during mashing or steeped like tea after fermentation to infuse the desired flavors into the final product. Rooibos is often employed in specialty beers such as red ales, Belgian-style witbiers, or even stouts where it complements roasted malt characters exceptionally well. With its versatility and flavorful qualities, Rooibos brings a touch of uniqueness to traditional beer styles while offering brewers endless possibilities for experimentation and creativity. Whether used as an infusion or added directly to the brew kettle, Rooibos provides an exciting twist on familiar beer styles that will surely entice adventurous drinkers seeking something new and delightful.

name: Saffron
notes: Saffron is the most expensive spice on Earth. This is because of the labour involved in growing and harvesting the spice. Saffron is the red-yellow stigma of the crocus flower and must be hand-picked during short annual flowering seasons. Each flower produces only three stigmas, so it takes approximately 150 flowers to yield just one gram of dry saffron threads.

name: Sanaam Chiles
notes: Sanaam chiles are red and flat, and are 2 to 4 inches in length. They have a medium-high heat.

name: Star Anise
notes: Star anise is undisputedly the prettiest spice of them all. Native to China and Vietnam, star anise is the fruit of an evergreen magnolia tree. The fruits are in the shape of an eight-pointed star, and each point holds a shiny brown seed. Star anise has a sweet, licoricey taste, and is used to flavour several liqueurs such as Sambuca, Galliano and pastis.

name: Tonka Beans
notes: Tonka beans are very unusual little beans that grow primarily in the northern part of South America. They share a lot of similarities with vanilla beans, to the point where they are sometimes used as a vanilla substitute. They are black and wrinkly, about an inch long, and have a sweet flavour that is like a combination of vanilla, cloves and cinnamon with a nuttiness reminiscent of almonds. Really delicious and unusual.

name: Vanilla
notes: Typical color range: 2-47 EBC (typical 12) Vanilla, a popular spice and herb, has found its way into the world of beer brewing, adding a delightful twist to various styles. Known for its sweet and creamy flavor profile with hints of caramel and floral undertones, Vanilla brings a unique richness to beers. When used in moderation, it can enhance the complexity and depth of flavors in both dark and light beers. Influencing the taste of beer, Vanilla imparts a smooth sweetness that balances well with different malt profiles. It adds an inviting aroma that complements the overall experience of drinking beer. Vanilla is commonly used as an adjunct ingredient during brewing or added through aging on oak barrels soaked in Vanilla extract or beans. Apart from its delectable taste characteristics, Vanilla possesses certain properties that make it favorable for use in beer production. Its natural oils contribute to improved head retention while lending a velvety mouthfeel to the brews. Additionally, vanillin compounds present in Vanilla act as antioxidants which help preserve the freshness of beers over time. Typical beer styles brewed with Vanilla include stouts, porters, brown ales, cream ales, Belgian quadrupels (Quad), and barleywines. These styles benefit from the addition of Vanilla by creating harmonious flavor combinations such as chocolate- Vanilla notes in stouts or caramel- Vanilla accents in porters.

name: Whisky
notes: Typical color range: 2-47 EBC (typical 3) Whisky, with its distinct flavor profile characterized by smoky, peaty, and caramel notes, has become a popular ingredient in beer brewing. Its influence on the taste of beer adds complexity and depth to the final product. When used in moderation, Whisky can enhance the maltiness of beers by imparting rich flavors that complement the existing ingredients. The application of Whisky in beer brewing is versatile and can be used for various purposes. It can be added during fermentation or aging to infuse unique characteristics into the beer. Whisky also acts as a preservative due to its high alcohol content and contributes to an extended shelf life for certain styles of beers. Properties such as oakiness from barrel aging or hints of vanilla from specific whiskies lend themselves well to certain beer styles. Scotch Ales benefit from the addition of Whisky as it complements their malty sweetness perfectly. Similarly, stouts and porters gain richness when aged in whiskey barrels or infused with whiskey itself.

name: White Pepper
notes: White Pepper, a popular spice in Asian cuisine, has also found its way into the world of beer brewing. Known for its pungent and slightly floral flavor profile, White Pepper adds a unique twist to beers by infusing them with hints of earthiness and heat. Its influence on the taste of beer can vary depending on the amount used; a small quantity might provide subtle undertones while larger amounts can create a more pronounced spiciness. White Pepper is typically added during the brewing process as an ingredient to enhance complexity and depth in certain beer styles. It pairs exceptionally well with Belgian-style beers such as saisons or farmhouse ales, where it complements the fruity esters produced by Belgian yeast strains. Additionally, this spice can be incorporated into other beer styles like stouts or wheat beers to introduce an unexpected element that tantalizes the palate. Apart from its distinct flavor characteristics, White Pepper possesses several properties that make it suitable for brewing applications. Firstly, it acts as a natural preservative due to its antimicrobial properties which help prolong shelf life. Furthermore, when used correctly in moderation, it contributes not only aromatic qualities but also aids in achieving balance within the overall flavor profile of the beer.
